items.title: Metals conduct heat AND electricity well because the same particles carry both
items.claim: Diamond is one of the best heat conductors known but doesn't conduct electricity. Copper is excellent at both. Wood is poor at both. The Wiedemann-Franz law links thermal and electrical conductivity of metals to a universal ratio.
items.prompt: Why is the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity nearly constant across metals?

options.text: Free electrons in a metal carry both heat and charge; the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity equals (pi squared over 3) times (k_B over e) squared times T — the Lorenz number — independent of which metal
Metals contain hidden phonons that scale with electrical conductivity

items.reveal_title: One sea of electrons does two jobs
items.reveal:
Metals have a sea of delocalised electrons free to move under an applied voltage (giving electrical conductivity) or under a temperature gradient (giving thermal conductivity).

The Wiedemann-Franz law (1853) predicts the ratio kappa/sigma = L * T, where L is the Lorenz number (about 2.44 x 10 to the minus 8 W ohm per K squared). Most metals at room temperature agree with this to within 10 percent.

Diamond breaks the pattern: it conducts heat via lattice vibrations (phonons) but has no free electrons. Wood is poor at both because it has neither significant free electrons nor an efficient phonon network.
items.why: Heat and electricity look like separate phenomena. In metals, the same charge carriers do both jobs — quantitatively.

items.title: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not zero
items.claim: Cool any substance and it gets denser as it approaches freezing — except water. Water reaches maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius and then becomes LESS dense as it cools further to 0 degrees Celsius.
items.prompt: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Trapped air bubbles make ice less dense than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice on freezing, so solid water occupies about 9 percent more volume than liquid water
Ice is colder, and colder things float
Surface tension on the underside of ice holds it up

items.reveal_title: Hydrogen bonding wins over packing efficiency
items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly, and molecules can crowd together. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral arrangement where each oxygen hydrogen-bonds to exactly four neighbours. That structure is open and roomy — about 9 percent more volume than the liquid.

This is why ponds freeze top-down rather than bottom-up. Fish survive winter because the densest water (4 degrees Celsius) sinks and the ice layer insulates everything below. If water behaved normally, lakes would freeze solid and life as we know it could not exist.
items.why: Students assume cooling always increases density. The hydrogen bond's geometry, not the temperature, controls the packing.

items.title: The hardest known natural substance and a pencil lead are the same element
items.claim: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs hardness scale. Graphite scores 1-2 (it leaves a streak on paper). Both are 100 percent pure carbon. Same element, same atoms, vastly different materials.

options.text: Diamond is sp3 hybridised with every carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others (a rigid 3D network); graphite is sp2 with strong in-plane bonds but only weak van der Waals forces between layers
Diamond and graphite have different isotopes of carbon

items.reveal:
In diamond every carbon shares electrons with four neighbours arranged at 109.5 degrees. The result is a giant covalent lattice that cannot be deformed without breaking strong sigma bonds in many directions at once.

In graphite each carbon bonds strongly to three neighbours in a flat hexagonal sheet. Sheets stack but are held together only by weak dispersion forces. Layers slide past each other easily — hence the pencil-streak behaviour.

Thermodynamically, graphite is actually the more stable form at room temperature and pressure by 2.9 kJ/mol. Diamond is metastable — it would convert to graphite, given long enough.
items.why: Identity of an element is not enough to determine properties. Bonding arrangement (allotropy) can transform a substance utterly.
